summary: SunVigator is a web tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare candidate landing sites near the Moon's south pole. The user picks a site (or enters custom coordinates), a start date and a 14 to 60 day window. The app computes where the Sun and Earth are relative to the local horizon and shows it three ways: a sky view with both bodies at a chosen moment, a time chart of their elevations, and a comparison table of all sites. Colored bars mark when the Sun is up (power generation) and when Earth is visible (direct-to-Earth communication). The table reports the share of time each is available, the share of time both are, and the longest continuous night. A horizon-mask slider approximates local terrain. Everything runs in the browser from a single HTML file with no backend, so complex illumination and communication geometry becomes quick to read for non-specialists.
details:
What it does: for a chosen lunar site and date window, the app shows Sun and Earth elevation and azimuth over time, flags periods with power (Sun above the horizon) and direct-to-Earth communication (Earth above the horizon), and ranks sites by the share of time both are available and by longest night.

How it works: Sun, Earth and Moon positions come from the astronomy-engine library. We convert the Earth and Sun directions into the Moon-fixed frame using the IAU lunar rotation model, build a local east/north/up basis at the site's latitude and longitude, and compute elevation and azimuth every 3 hours. We checked the result against the library's own libration values: the sub-Earth point matched to about 0.02 degrees, and the Sun's elevation at the pole stayed within the expected +/-1.5 degree seasonal range.

Benefits: planners and the public can compare sites and dates in seconds instead of using complicated interfaces. The horizon-mask slider shows how a few degrees of local terrain change power and communication availability.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, SVG charts, astronomy-engine (MIT license). No backend.

Limitations and next steps: the model uses a smooth horizon and approximate site coordinates. A next step is loading real horizon profiles derived from LRO LOLA elevation data for each site.

Creativity: one view combines the sky, a time chart and a site ranking, and it works on a phone.
